source: Atlassian, 'The State of Developer Experience in 2026' (report PDF, 24 numbered pages, cover subtitle 'The AI experiment is over. The hard part of operationalizing it has just begun.'; PDF created 14 Oct 2026). Foreword by Taroon Mandhana, Chief Technology Officer, AI & Teamwork. Opened: landing page https://www.atlassian.com/teams/software-development/state-of-developer-experience-2026 and the full PDF linked from it, https://dam-cdn.atl.orangelogic.com/CDNLink/AT12P1R5.pdf. Secondary opened: Steef-Jan Wiggers, 'Developers Reporting Double-Digit Weekly Time Savings from AI Fell from 68% to 26%', InfoQ, Oct 27, 2026, https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/10/atlassian-devex-2026/
data_type: Survey (self-report), with two callouts citing separate Atlassian DX telemetry research (Q2 2026 State of AI Impact in Engineering, sample from 500+ companies).
sample_and_method: Methodology page: 'This report draws on survey responses from 1,155 individual contributors and 405 engineering leaders, collected in 2026 across a range of organization sizes, industries, and geographies.' No fieldwork dates, recruitment method, panel provider, country list or weighting published. Landing page describes it as 'a survey of 1,500+ software practitioners'. InfoQ notes the 2025 edition surveyed 3,500 developers and managers across six countries, so year-on-year comparisons use a different, larger base.
vendor_interest: Yes, strong. Atlassian sells developer tooling (Jira, Bitbucket, Pipelines, Rovo AI) and owns DX, a product marketed on the landing page as 'Measure productivity and AI impact'. The report recommends the DX Core 4 framework and an Atlassian DX AI measurement framework, and its central recommendation (formalize AI-native delivery through an 'engineering system of work' with shared context and a 'shared system of record') aligns with Atlassian's products. InfoQ flags this: 'vendor research from a company selling developer tooling, arriving at a conclusion that favors formalizing AI delivery'.
headline_figures: Executive summary: 'Nearly everyone in this year's survey, 95% of developers and 96% of engineering leaders say their organization actively uses AI in engineering'; 'Developers still report meaningful local benefit from AI: 87% say it helps them ship work faster, and 80% say it helps them deliver more without longer hours.'; 'In 2025, 68% of developers reported saving 10 or more hours a week with AI. In 2026, that figure is 26%.' Chapter 1: 'Only 28% of developers say they have noticeably less friction than before AI; 50% say they have about the same friction'. Time table (developers / leaders): 'Spend 4+ hours per week managing AI tools' 49% / 57%; 'I spend time correcting AI-generated work that missed original intent' 65% / 72%; 'Save 11+ hours per week using AI' 26% / 31%. '29% of developers say reviewing or managing AI-generated code and output is a source of friction.' Snapshot: '60% of developers say AI use is treated as a productivity signal in their organization'; '42% of leaders say they have the right metrics to separate real gains from activity'. Chapter 4 panel: developers 60% 'say greater AI use is treated as a signal of productivity', 41% 'say they sometimes use AI more than necessary because they feel expected to', 68% 'say greater AI use does not accurately reflect the value they deliver', 85% 'say they know when AI tools genuinely help versus create extra work'; leaders 64% 'say greater AI use correlates with better outcomes', 59% 'worry about performative AI use', 81% 'agree that measuring AI use can create the wrong incentives', 42% 'say they have the right metrics to distinguish genuine gains from inflated AI activity.' Strategy: 17% of developers and 23% of leaders report a clear, actively implemented AI strategy across the SDLC; 41% of developers with such a strategy report noticeably less friction vs 22% with an inconsistent or poorly communicated one.
metric_layer: Input/usage (adoption, AI use treated as signal) and self-reported activity/output (ship faster, deliver more, hours saved, hours managing AI), plus perceived quality (59%/60% say output higher quality; 73% say speed can cost quality). The report itself says it does not measure delivery or financial outcomes: findings are 'not system-level telemetry such as deployment frequency, cycle time, or revenue impact.' One telemetry callout (DX, 500+ companies, Q1 to Q2 2026): code maintainability +3.8%, change confidence -6.1%.
respondent_role_split: Developers (ICs, n=1,155) vs engineering leaders (n=405) throughout; no director/executive split. Examples: ship faster 87% / 88%; deliver more without longer hours 80% / 77%; save 11+ hours 26% / 31%; 4+ hours managing AI 49% / 57%; correcting AI work that missed intent 65% / 72%; clear AI strategy 17% / 23%. Measurement table (leaders 'How are you measuring developer productivity?' vs developers 'What is the best way...'): hours worked 37% / 17%; story points 36% / 26%; code volume 35% / 17%; deployment frequency 35% / 19%; AI tool usage 26% / 12%; SPACE 20% / 41%; 'can't/shouldn't be measured' 16% / 33%. Seniority split among developers: saves 11+ hours 21% junior, 27% software engineer, 28% senior; AI officially standardized 8% / 21% / 26%. Leaders on hiring: '37% say they have hired fewer junior developers in the past 12 months.'
workload_signal: '49% of developers say they spend 4+ hours per week reviewing AI output, correcting prompts, and more' (landing page); table wording 'Spend 4+ hours per week managing AI tools' 49% developers, 57% leaders. 65% of developers (72% leaders) spend time correcting AI work that missed original intent. 18% 'lose time configuring and training AI to reliably work within their workflows.' Pressure to use AI: 41% of developers 'sometimes use AI more than necessary because they feel expected to'. Counter-signal: 80% say AI helps them deliver more without longer hours. Report: 'Managing AI itself is becoming a significant addition to a developer's workweek.' No burnout measure. 66% of developers say leadership does not fully understand their challenges (44% in 2024, 63% in 2025).
definition_of_value_offered: Yes, explicitly. Chapter 4, 'Measuring AI impact without mistaking activity for value': AI's 'most visible signals—tool use, token consumption, generated output, and code volume—are also the easiest to count, game, and remain weak evidence that engineering is creating more value.' Recommends outcome questions: 'Are teams delivering valuable changes with greater confidence? Are developers spending less time waiting for context, approvals, or information? Is quality improving without creating hidden review or rework burdens? Are teams able to invest more in new capabilities rather than maintenance and overhead? Are engineers gaining the judgment required to direct, evaluate, and safely use AI?' Telemetry such as adoption, token use, accepted suggestions and agent activity are 'diagnostic signals, not proof of success. A rise in AI usage is meaningful only when leaders can connect it to impact and outcomes.' Points to DX Core 4 (speed, effectiveness, quality, business impact) and a DX framework of AI utilization, cost and impact.
removal_counterfactual: None. No comparison of teams or periods without AI tools. Only adjacent figure: 'only 2% say they don't currently use AI at all'. Before/after comparisons are respondents' own recall ('noticeably less friction than before AI').
key_quotes: 1. 'Developer productivity measurement—an already fraught conversation—is at even greater risk of rewarding AI usage over impact' (report snapshot heading; contains em dashes, paraphrase for site use). 2. 'Those questions are harder to answer than "How often is the tool used?", which is precisely why they matter.' (report, chapter 4)
caveats: Self-report survey by a vendor with products in this space; the report says findings 'should not be interpreted as causal proof' and are not telemetry. No fieldwork dates or recruitment detail. Year-on-year comparison bases differ (2025: 3,500 respondents across six countries per InfoQ; 2026: 1,560). Internal inconsistencies in the PDF: the 2026 hours-saved figure appears as '10 or more hours' 26% (exec summary), '10+ hours' 25% (chapter 1) and 'Save 11+ hours' 26% (table), so the threshold and figure are not stable; quality appears as 60% (chapter 1) and 59% (speed-quality section); juniors citing more cross-functional coordination are 62% 'vs 56% overall' in text, but the role table gives 29% of developers for 'More cross-functional coordination and communication' while the seniority table gives 55% for mid-level engineers. Landing page/PDF conflict: landing page says '75% of developers say they have more responsibility for validating the quality and safety of AI-generated output', but the PDF role table gives 41% developers / 37% leaders for that statement; treat 75% as unverified. Landing page frames the 64% leaders figure under 'AI usage is—incorrectly—being treated as a productivity signal', whereas the 60% figure is the developers' 'productivity signal' item; InfoQ uses the 60% developer figure correctly. Landing page sample '1,500+' vs PDF 1,560.
access: Primary opened in full: landing page text and all 26 pages of the PDF (image-based PDF, read page by page visually). InfoQ write-up opened in full and its figures checked against the PDF. Not verified: the separate DX Q2 2026 AI Impact report telemetry, and the 2025 edition's 68% figure and sample (taken from this report and InfoQ, not the 2025 report itself).
